title: Measuring forces and friction
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 3 Physics: push and pull, changing shape, how big is that force?, forcemeters, friction. No textbook needed.
summary: A push can be measured, just like a length. Your child draws forces as arrows, builds a forcemeter from a rubber band and measures forces in newtons. They learn the difference between mass (how much stuff) and weight (how hard the Earth pulls it). Then they test friction: the force that slows things, makes heat and wears things out, but also lets us walk, write and hold on. They find out why rolling is so much easier than sliding.
builds_on: Class 1: pushes and pulls; things don't start or stop by themselves; every push gets a push back; rubbing slows things. Class 2: the four jobs of a force, elastic and plastic, a bigger pull makes a bigger stretch, speed, falling and air resistance. Next: Class 4 uses forces in balance, simple machines, pressure and floating; Class 5 adds them all up in force diagrams, with air and water resistance, terminal speed and rockets.
subconcepts: forces have a size and a direction, drawn as arrows
the support force: a table pushes up on a book
small, medium and large forces, put in order
the newton (N), and how a forcemeter measures it
springs stretch in step with the pull (why forcemeters work)
mass and weight: kilograms of stuff, newtons of pull
forces change shape: a bigger force, a bigger change
friction acts where two surfaces rub, against the movement
rough and smooth surfaces, and heavier things pressing harder
friction makes heat and wears things away
rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction: wheels, rollers, ball bearings
making friction bigger (treads, grip, sand) or smaller (oil, polish, water)
goals: By the end your child can draw forces as arrows showing size and direction, and say whether forces are balanced or unbalanced.
By the end your child can build and read a forcemeter, measure forces in newtons, and put forces in order of size.
By the end your child can explain the difference between mass and weight, and say what would happen to their weight on the Moon.
By the end your child can plan and carry out a fair test of friction on different surfaces, repeat measurements and say what they found.
By the end your child can explain why rolling is easier than sliding, and give ways to make friction bigger and smaller.
By the end your child can give examples of friction as a help and as a problem, and name people whose knowledge of friction was left out of the books.
words: force
a push or a pull. It has a size and a direction.
balanced forces
forces that cancel each other out, so nothing changes
support force
the push up from a surface on whatever rests on it
newton (N)
the unit we measure force in. A 100 g packet of dal pulls down with about 1 newton.
forcemeter
a tool with a spring that measures forces in newtons
mass
how much stuff something is made of, measured in grams and kilograms
weight
how hard gravity pulls on something, measured in newtons
friction
a force between two surfaces rubbing together that acts against the movement
lubricant
something slippery, like oil, that reduces friction
ball bearing
small steel balls that let wheels roll instead of rub
fair test
a test where only one thing changes
repeat
to do a test again to make sure the result is right

days.title: Forces have size and direction
days.goal: Recall what forces do, then show their size and direction with arrows and decide when they balance.

steps.title: Four jobs quiz
steps.do: Ask: 'What can a force do?' (Start or stop, speed up or slow down, change direction, change shape.) 'What is elastic? Plastic?' Then ask your child to show you a force that does two jobs at once (kicking a rolling ball sideways: changes direction and speed). Ask: 'True or false: you can push something without it pushing back on you?' (False. Every push gets a push back.)

steps.title: Arrow drawings
steps.do: Draw a box on a sheet. Ask your child to push a real box gently, then hard. Draw a short arrow for the gentle push and a long arrow for the hard push, starting on the box and pointing the way the push went. Then draw tug of war: two arrows pointing opposite ways. Ask: 'If the arrows are the same length, what happens?' (Nothing moves: the forces are balanced.) 'If one is longer?' (The rope moves that way: unbalanced.) Say: 'Every force has two things: how big it is and which way it goes. An arrow shows both.'

steps.title: Balanced or unbalanced?
steps.do: Do Activity a1: a book pushed from both sides with one finger each, a hanging bag, and a tug of war. Each time your child decides: balanced (nothing changes) or unbalanced (something starts, stops, speeds up, slows or turns), and draws the arrows.

steps.title: Are there forces when nothing moves?
steps.do: Point at a book lying still on the table. Ask: 'Are there any forces on this book?' Many children say no. Hint: 'Why doesn't it fall?' The Earth pulls it down (gravity) and the table pushes it up (the support force; scientists also call it the normal force). Show it: lay a thin plastic ruler across two tins and put the book on it. The ruler bends. Say: 'The table bends too, but too little to see. Its atoms are squeezed together, and squeezed atoms push back. That push is the support force. Without it, the book would fall towards the centre of the Earth.' Draw the book with two equal arrows, one up and one down.

need: a thin plastic ruler and two tins

days.title: Make a forcemeter
days.goal: Build a rubber-band forcemeter and mark it in newtons.

steps.title: Guess the pull
steps.do: Hand your child a 100 g packet (tea, rava or dal), then a 1 kg packet of rice. Ask: 'How many times harder does the big one pull down on your hand?' Let them guess. (Ten times.) Ask: 'How could we measure a pull instead of guessing?' Remind them of last year's rubber band: more coins, more stretch.

steps.title: Build the forcemeter
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Use a 100 g packet to mark 1 N, two packets for 2 N, and so on. A 100 g packet pulls down with very nearly 1 newton. Ask as you go: 'Are the marks evenly spaced?' (Nearly, because the band stretches in step with the pull, as Hooke found.)

steps.title: Meet Isaac Newton, and the apple
steps.do: Say: 'The newton is named after Isaac Newton, an English scientist who explained how forces make things move.' Ask: 'Did an apple really fall on his head?' Listen. Then say: 'Newton told a friend that seeing an apple fall in his garden got him thinking. Nobody wrote that it hit his head. That part was added later.' Ask: 'Who else's work did Newton build on?' (Galileo, Hooke and many others.)

steps.title: Try it
steps.do: Your child measures the pull of three things with their forcemeter: a pencil box, a water bottle, a shoe. Write each in newtons. Ask: 'Which pulls down hardest?'

need: small bag or cup with string

days.title: Mass and weight
days.goal: Tell apart how much stuff something has (mass) from how hard the Earth pulls it (weight).

steps.title: Kilograms or newtons?
steps.do: Ask: 'When we buy 1 kg of rice, are we buying a pull?' Let them think. Say: 'Kilograms tell us how much stuff there is. Scientists call that mass. Newtons tell us how hard the Earth pulls it. That pull is called weight. At the shop we mix them up, and that is fine. Scientists keep them apart.'

steps.title: Weigh and pull
steps.do: Do Experiment e3: put five things on a kitchen scale and write their mass in grams, then hang each from the forcemeter and write the pull in newtons. Ask: 'Do you see a pattern?' (About 1 N for every 100 g.) 'So what would 1 kg of rice pull with?' (About 10 N.)

steps.title: Your weight on the Moon
steps.do: If you have a bathroom scale, your child stands on it and reads the number. Then they push down hard on a table beside them: the number drops. They bend their knees quickly: the number jumps about. Ask: 'Did you get lighter or heavier?' (No. The amount of you didn't change.) Say: 'The scale doesn't feel gravity. It feels how hard you press on it, and it pushes back the same. That push is what it shows.' Then ask: 'If you went to the Moon, would there be less of you?' (No, your mass stays the same.) 'Would the Moon pull you as hard?' (No, about one sixth as hard.) Work it out: a 30 kg child pulls down on Earth with about 300 N; on the Moon about 50 N. 'How high could you jump on the Moon?' (About six times higher.)

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1 sections A and B: arrows, balanced forces, reading forcemeters and mass versus weight. Section C is for Day 5.

need: five small things with handles or in a bag

days.title: Small forces, big forces, new shapes
days.goal: Put forces in order of size and do a fair test of how a bigger force changes a shape more.

steps.title: Put forces in order
steps.do: Write on slips: pressing a phone screen, lifting a school bag, opening a fridge, pushing a car, an ant pulling a crumb, kicking a football, a crane lifting a lorry. Your child lays them in a line from smallest to biggest force. Ask: 'Which ones could we measure with our forcemeter? Which are too big?' (Pushing a car would need a forcemeter of hundreds of newtons.)

steps.title: The clay drop test
steps.do: Do Experiment e4: drop equal clay balls from three heights onto a tile and measure the flat patch each makes. Before testing, ask: 'What must we keep the same?' (Same size ball, same clay, same tile, drop not throw.) 'What do we change?' (Only the height.) Record in a table.

steps.title: What did we find?
steps.do: Ask: 'Which drop made the biggest flat patch? Why?' (From higher up it was going faster when it hit, so the tile pushed back harder to stop it, and squashed it more.) 'Would a rubber ball keep the flat patch?' (No, it's elastic.)

steps.title: Shapes in the kitchen
steps.do: Ask your child to show three shape-changing forces in the kitchen and say whether each is small or big: rolling chapati dough (medium), squeezing a lemon (medium), crushing garlic with a stone (big), tearing a curry leaf (small).

days.title: What is friction?
days.goal: Feel friction, measure it, and find that it makes heat and wears things away.

steps.title: Rub your hands
steps.do: Rub your palms together fast for 10 seconds. Ask: 'What do you feel?' (Warm.) 'Now rub with soap and water. Easier or harder?' (Easier.) Say: 'The force that acts when surfaces rub is called friction. It always pushes against the way things are moving. It slows things down and makes heat.'

steps.title: Drag test
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Hook the forcemeter to a shoe and drag it slowly and steadily across the floor. Read the force while it's moving, not at the jerk at the start. Do it three times each with 0, 1 and 2 packets in the shoe.

steps.title: Why repeat?
steps.do: Ask: 'We dragged each shoe three times. Were the numbers exactly the same?' (Probably not.) 'Why do scientists repeat tests?' (To check the result wasn't an accident, and to take the middle value.) Circle the middle value in each row.

steps.title: Friction makes heat and wear
steps.do: Rub an eraser hard on paper 20 times and touch it: warm. Look at the soles of old chappals, a worn step, a pencil tip. Ask: 'Where did the missing rubber, stone and lead go?' (Rubbed off in tiny bits by friction.) Then do section C of Worksheet ws1 together.

days.title: Rough and smooth
days.goal: Do a fair test of friction on different surfaces, test Leonardo's surprise, and hear the story.

steps.title: Story: Arjun's Wish
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'What went wrong when there was no friction?' and 'Arjun said friction was also what let him hold on. What did he mean?'

steps.title: Surface test
steps.do: Do Experiment e2: drag the same shoe with one packet inside across tiles, a cotton floor mat, a towel, a doormat and a steel plate, measuring the force three times on each. Ask: 'What did we keep the same?' (Shoe, weight, pulling slowly.) 'Which surface needed the biggest force? Why?' (Rough surfaces have more bumps that catch on each other.)

steps.title: Leonardo's surprise
steps.do: Talk about voice v1: Leonardo da Vinci found that friction hardly depends on how big the touching face is. Then test his claim: drag a brick-shaped box of books on its big face, then on its thin side, with the forcemeter. Ask: 'Did the touching area change the friction?' (Usually hardly at all.) Ask the voice's question.

need: the same shoe with one packet
tiles, a cotton floor mat, a towel, a doormat, a steel plate

days.title: Rolling beats sliding
days.goal: Discover that rolling has far less friction than sliding, and use it to move a heavy load.

steps.title: Socks and chappals
steps.do: On a smooth floor, your child slides in socks, then tries in rubber chappals. Ask: 'Which gave more grip? Why?' (Rubber has more friction.) 'Why do chappal soles have a pattern?' (Treads grip the ground and push water out of the way.)

steps.title: Marble bearings
steps.do: Put a heavy book flat on the table and try to spin it with one finger: hard. Now put a tin lid on the table, rim up, and fill it with marbles. Put the book on the marbles and spin it again: it turns easily. Ask: 'What changed?' (The marbles roll instead of the book rubbing.) Say: 'This is how ball bearings work, in cycles, fans and car wheels. Rolling has much less friction than sliding.'

steps.title: Project: move Paati's trunk
steps.do: Say: 'Paati (Grandma) has a heavy trunk to move across the room, and she can't lift it.' Use a box full of books as the trunk. Your child tests sliding, rollers (round pencils or rolling pins), a cloth underneath and toy-car wheels, measuring the force for each three times with the forcemeter. Help them keep it fair: same box, same floor, pull slowly. Ask: 'Which needed the smallest force? Why was the wheel such a big invention?'

need: a tin lid and 15 marbles (or round dried peas)
round pencils or two rolling pins

days.title: Friction: friend or foe?
days.goal: Find where friction helps and where it gets in the way, and weigh up an ancient puzzle.

steps.title: Friction Rally
steps.do: Play the Friction Rally board game (g1). On each square your child must say whether friction is helping or causing trouble, and why, before following the square. Afterwards, your child dances for 30 seconds in socks on a smooth floor, then in bare feet, and freezes when you clap. Ask: 'In which could you stop at once? Why?' (Bare feet. They have more friction.)

steps.title: Pouring water on sand
steps.do: Talk about voice v2. A tomb painting in Egypt shows a giant statue on a sledge being pulled over sand while someone pours liquid in front. Ask: 'Why would you pour water on sand?' Then try it if you can get a little sand (from a plant shop or a building site): drag a small box over dry sand and over slightly damp sand in a tray, using the forcemeter. If you have no sand, just talk about it. Ask the voice's question.

steps.title: Friend or foe sheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2: sort where friction helps and where it is a problem, choose how people increase or reduce it, and build the force diagrams.

need: the printed board game, a die and counters
a tray of dry sand and a cup of water (if you can get sand)

days.title: Review and teach it back
days.goal: Pull it all together: arrows, newtons, mass and weight, friction.

steps.title: Challenge sheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 together. Read aloud and let your child reason out loud before writing.

steps.title: Big questions
steps.do: Pick two big questions: 'What would the world be like with no friction at all?' (You couldn't walk, write, tie a knot or stop a car; things would slide for ever.) 'Is there friction in space?' (Not between a spacecraft and empty space, but there is inside its machines.) Read the perspective about women who carry water on their heads, and ask its question.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches you how to use the forcemeter, the difference between mass and weight, and what friction is, using the things from this week. Ask the check questions as a curious student. Finish: 'Show me one way to make more friction and one way to make less.'

need: the forcemeter, shoe and box from this week

sections.p: A book lies still on a table. Show both forces.
A bag hangs still from the forcemeter. Show both forces.
sections.obj: a bag hanging from a forcemeter

sections.p: In a tug of war, Team A pulls harder than Team B. What happens?
opts: the rope moves towards team A
the rope moves towards team B

sections.p: Balanced or unbalanced?
items: a book lying on a shelf
a ball speeding down a slope
a fan hanging from the ceiling
a tug of war where nobody moves

sections.p: Forces are measured in ____.
A 100 g packet pulls down with about ____ newton.
Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: how hard gravity pulls, in newtons

sections.p: On the Moon, what happens to you?
opts: your mass and weight both stay the same
your mass stays the same but your weight is about one sixth
you have no mass at all

sections.p: A book on a table isn't moving. Why doesn't it fall through the table?
Why do we repeat each measurement three times?
Is friction helping or causing a problem?
items: a rope burning your hands in tug of war

sections.p: Does it make friction bigger or smaller?
You drag a shoe to the right at a steady speed. Show the pull and the friction.
sections.obj: a shoe dragged across the floor at steady speed

sections.p: A cycle rolls to the right and brakes. Which way does the friction from the brakes act?
A box is pushed hard to the right and speeds up. Show the push and the friction.
sections.obj: a box being pushed and speeding up

sections.p: In the trunk project, you moved a heavy box of books. Which way needed the smallest force?
opts: rolling it on wheels or rollers

sections.p: Why do ball bearings make a fan or a cycle wheel turn more easily?
Old bullock carts had wooden wheels turning on wooden axles. People greased the axles with oil. What would happen if they didn't?
In the story, Arjun wished there was no friction. Write three things that would go wrong in your house, and one thing that would be better.
Plan a fair test: do new chappals grip a wet floor better than old, worn ones? Say what you would change, what you would keep the same and what you would measure.
Your forcemeter reads 5 N on Earth for a bag of rice. What would it read on the Moon? Is there less rice?
When you start to drag a heavy box, the forcemeter jumps up, then drops a little while it slides. What does that tell you?
opts: starting to slide takes more force than keeping it sliding

sections.p: A child walks to the right. Which way does the floor's friction push the child's foot? (Think: the foot pushes back on the floor.)
sections.obj: a walking child's foot on the floor

sections.p: A book sits still on a sloping board. It doesn't slide down to the left. Which way does friction act?
sections.obj: a book resting on a ramp that slopes down to the left

sections.p: Leonardo da Vinci, an Italian artist and scientist, tested blocks sliding on a table. He found that friction depends mostly on what?
opts: how big the touching face is
how hard the surfaces press together

sections.p: Why do two very flat, smooth sheets of glass with a little water between them stick hard?
opts: very smooth surfaces touch in many more places, so they grip

experiments.title: Drag test
experiments.question: Does a heavier shoe need a bigger force to drag?
steps: Hook the forcemeter to the shoe's lace or heel.
Pull slowly and steadily along the floor. Read the force while it's moving.
Do it three times and write all three.
Add one packet inside. Repeat three times.
Add a second packet. Repeat.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the heavier shoe need more, less or the same force?'
experiments.observe: The force in newtons for each try. Notice too that the reading jumps higher just as the shoe starts to move.
experiments.why: A heavier shoe presses down on the floor harder, so the bumps of the two surfaces dig in more and friction is bigger. You need a bigger pull to keep it moving. Getting it started takes a little more force than keeping it going, because still surfaces settle into each other.

experiments.title: Surface test
experiments.question: Which surface has the most friction?
need: the same shoe with one packet
4–5 surfaces: tiles, a cotton floor mat, a towel, a doormat, a steel plate
steps: Put the shoe on the first surface.
Pull slowly and steadily. Read the force while it's moving.
Repeat three times. Write the middle value.
Do the same on each surface.
Put the surfaces in order from most to least friction.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to put the surfaces in order before testing.
experiments.why: Every surface has tiny bumps, even ones that feel smooth. When two surfaces rub, the bumps catch and grip. Rough surfaces like a doormat catch more; smooth ones like steel catch less.

experiments.title: Weigh and pull
experiments.question: How is a mass in grams linked to a pull in newtons?
need: five things: a 100 g packet, a 200 g packet, a small water bottle, a shoe, a pencil box
a bag to hang them in
steps: Put each thing on the kitchen scale and write its mass in grams.
Hang the same thing from the forcemeter in the bag and write the pull in newtons.
Make a table: thing, grams, newtons.
Look for a pattern.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'If 100 g pulls with 1 N, what will 200 g pull with?'
experiments.observe: Grams and newtons for each thing.
experiments.why: On Earth, every 100 g of stuff is pulled down with about 1 newton (more exactly 0.98 N). The scale is set up to tell you how much stuff (mass); the forcemeter tells you how hard the Earth pulls it (weight). On the Moon there would be just as much stuff, but the forcemeter would read only about a sixth as much, because the Moon pulls more weakly.

experiments.title: The clay drop test
experiments.question: Does a bigger force change a shape more?
steps: Make three balls of clay exactly the same size (weigh them or use the same spoonful).
Drop the first from 25 cm above the tile. Don't throw it.
Drop the second from 50 cm, and the third from 100 cm.
Measure across the flat patch on each ball in millimetres.
Write a table and repeat once with new balls.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which ball will have the biggest flat patch?'
experiments.observe: The width of the flattened patch on each ball.
experiments.why: A ball dropped from higher is moving faster when it hits, so the tile has to push harder to stop it. That bigger push squashes the clay more. Clay is plastic, so it keeps the squashed shape for us to measure. A rubber ball would squash too, but it springs back.

activities.title: Balanced or unbalanced?
steps: Push a book from both sides with one finger each, equally hard. Does it move?
Push harder on one side. What happens?
Hold a bag still. Which forces are acting? (Your hand pulls up, gravity pulls down.)
Play tug of war with an old towel. When does the towel move?
Draw arrows for each.
activities.outcome: Your child can say forces are balanced when nothing changes and unbalanced when something starts, stops or changes.

activities.title: Home-made forcemeter
need: small bag or cup with string
steps: Tape the rubber band to the top of the card strip so it hangs down along it.
Open a paper clip into a hook and hang it from the rubber band. Hang the bag from the hook.
Mark where the bottom of the band is with no load: write 0 N.
Add one 100 g packet. Mark the new position: 1 N.
Add packets one at a time, marking 2 N, 3 N, 4 N.
Hold the top and test it on things around the house.
activities.outcome: A working forcemeter marked in newtons.

project.title: Move Paati's trunk
steps: Load a box with books so it's heavy.
Measure the force to drag it on the floor, three times.
Try three ways to reduce friction: rollers, a cloth on a smooth floor, wheels.
Measure each, three times, and circle the middle value.
Make a bar chart of the results and choose the best design.
Present it to the family: what worked, and why?
project.outcome: A tested design and a bar chart, explained to the family.

game.title: Friction Rally
rules: Read your square aloud. Say whether friction is helping or causing trouble, and why.
Good reason: follow the square's move. No reason: stay where you are.
squares: New tyre treads grip the road: +2
Bald tyres on a wet road: back 2
Squeaky hinge: oil it, miss a turn
Rubber chappals on a wet floor: +1
Rope burn in tug of war: back 1
Oily hands drop a steel tumbler: back 1

big: What would the world be like with no friction at all?
Why did it take people so long to invent the wheel, and why did some great civilisations not use it much?
If your weight changes from planet to planet, what is the real 'you' that stays the same?
Should the people who carry heavy loads every day be called experts in forces?

challenge.q: The famous story says an apple fell on Isaac Newton's head and he discovered gravity. Is that true?
challenge.hint: Newton told a friend, William Stukeley, many years later, that seeing an apple fall in his garden got him thinking about why things always fall straight down. Nobody recorded it hitting his head. That part was added later. And his ideas took about 20 years of hard work, building on Galileo, Kepler, Hooke and others, not one moment. Ask: why do people like 'one big moment' stories?

challenge.q: We say smooth surfaces have less friction. Is that always true?
challenge.hint: Two very smooth, flat pieces of glass or steel can stick together surprisingly hard. Very smooth isn't always slippery. Try two smooth plastic rulers pressed together with a drop of water.

challenge.q: People say 'I weigh 30 kilograms'. Is that right?
challenge.hint: Strictly, kilograms measure mass (how much of you there is). Your weight is the pull of gravity on you, about 300 newtons on Earth. Everyone says kilograms in daily life, and that's fine. But on the Moon your kilograms stay the same and your newtons drop to about 50.

perspectives.who: A worker at a wooden oil press (chekku)
perspectives.view: In a chekku, a wooden pole grinds sesame or coconut inside a wooden bowl to press out oil. Wooden presses and bullock-cart axles were greased with oil so they would not squeak and wear out. Ask: why does oil help?
Climbers rub chalk on their hands to get more grip. Ask: why would a dry hand hold better than a sweaty one?

perspectives.who: Women who carry water on their heads
perspectives.view: In many villages in India and Africa, women carry heavy pots of water on their heads, balanced on a cloth ring. In 1986, scientists studying women in Kenya found they could carry loads of up to a fifth of their body weight using almost no extra energy. Army recruits carrying the same load in backpacks could not do this. Ask: how do you think the women learned it?

A gecko hunts insects on walls and ceilings, so it must not fall. Its toes have millions of tiny hairs. They get so close to a surface that tiny forces between atoms hold the gecko on, even on glass. Ask: what could people learn from a gecko?

perspectives.who: An ice skater and a kabaddi player
perspectives.view: A skater wants almost no friction, so she can glide. A kabaddi player in bare feet on mud wants lots of grip to stop and turn. Ask: is friction good or bad, or does it depend on what you want to do?

voices.who: Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519), Italy, and Guillaume Amontons (1663–1705), France
voices.idea: Leonardo wrote in his notebooks that the friction on a block doesn't depend on how much of it touches the surface, only on how heavy it is. His notebooks weren't published, so the idea was lost. About 200 years later, Amontons found the same rules again and published them in 1699.
voices.then: Many scientists didn't believe it at first. Surely a bigger touching area means more rubbing? Charles-Augustin de Coulomb tested it carefully in 1781 and confirmed it.
voices.now: Accepted for most everyday solid things. Scientists now know why: surfaces only really touch at their tiny bumps, and the true touching area depends on the weight, not the size of the face. The rules are still called Amontons' laws, though Leonardo found them first.
voices.ask: We dragged the box on its big face and its thin side. Is Leonardo right? Who should the rules be named after: the first to find them, or the first to publish?

voices.who: Daniel Bonn and colleagues (2014), University of Amsterdam, about ancient Egypt
voices.idea: A wall painting in the tomb of Djehutihotep (about 1900 BCE) shows workers pulling a huge statue on a sledge over sand, with one person pouring liquid in front. In 2014 Bonn's team showed in the lab that sand wet with the right amount of water needs about half the pulling force of dry sand, because the water makes sand grains stick together into a firmer surface.
voices.then: Some scholars had thought the pouring was a religious ritual. The new study gave a physical reason.
voices.now: The physics of wet sand is well accepted. Whether the Egyptians poured water for this reason, for ritual, or both, can't be proved from one painting. Either way, the workers who learned the trick by doing it are not named anywhere.
voices.ask: What evidence would you need to be sure why the person in the painting was pouring water?

books.title: Newton and Me
books.author: Lynne Mayer
books.why: A boy and his dog discover forces and friction while playing, in rhyme.

books.title: Who Was Isaac Newton?
books.author: Janet B. Pascal
books.why: Newton's real life, including the true apple story.

books.title: The Way Things Work Now
books.author: David Macaulay
books.why: Beautiful drawings of wheels, levers and machines that fight or use friction. Dip into the wheel and friction pages together.

check.q: What does a longer force arrow mean? What does it mean when two arrows are equal and opposite?
check.a: A longer arrow means a bigger force. Equal and opposite arrows mean the forces are balanced, so nothing changes.

check.q: What do we measure forces in, and with what?
What's the difference between mass and weight?
check.a: Mass is how much stuff, in kilograms. Weight is how hard gravity pulls it, in newtons. On the Moon your mass stays the same and your weight is about a sixth.

check.q: What is friction, and which way does it act?
check.a: Friction is a force between surfaces that rub together. It acts against the movement.

check.q: Which has more friction: a doormat or a steel plate? Why?
check.a: The doormat. Its rough bumps catch on the shoe more.

check.q: Why is rolling easier than sliding?
check.a: Rolling things don't rub along the surface, so there's much less friction.

check.q: In our surface test, what did we keep the same and what did we change?
check.a: We kept the same shoe, the same weight and the same slow pull. We changed only the surface.

check.q: A book lies still on a table. Are there forces on it?
check.a: Yes: gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up. They are balanced.

story.title: Arjun's Wish
text: Arjun's cycle was old and heavy, and the road to school went up a hill, and every morning he hated it. "If only nothing ever rubbed," he said, puffing, his legs burning. "If only wheels slid along like butter. If only there were no friction at all."
That evening, sitting on the roof, he saw a small gecko on the warm wall. It looked at him with its golden eyes. "Is that your wish?" said the gecko. "No more rubbing? No more friction, anywhere?"
"Then sleep," said the gecko, "and in the morning, we shall see."

In the morning Arjun swung his legs out of bed, stood up, and immediately fell flat on his back. His feet had shot out from under him as if the floor were made of ice. He tried to crawl, but his hands slid. He grabbed the bed, but his fingers slipped off it like wet soap. Everything was slippery. Everything.

From the kitchen came a clatter and a cry: Amma's steel plate had slid off the counter, and the dosas were skating across the floor. His little sister's hair ribbons slithered out of their knots and floated to the ground. Downstairs, a scooter that tried to brake simply kept going, sliding gently and helplessly down the lane.

Arjun lay on the floor and tried to think. He reached for his school notebook to write down what was happening, the way his teacher said scientists do. But the pencil slid across the page and left no mark at all, not a single grey line. Without rubbing, the pencil couldn't leave any of itself behind. His shoelaces had untied themselves and lay like two limp worms. Even the knot in the clothes line on the balcony had slipped apart, and all the washing lay in a heap below.

Outside, the women at the tap were trying to carry their water pots home. Arjun had seen them every day of his life, walking tall and straight with the pots on their heads, on a little cloth ring that held them steady. But this morning the pots slid off the rings, and the rings slid off their heads, and water went everywhere.

Arjun's Paati, his grandmother, was the worst. She was old and her legs were weak, and every day he held her hand to help her down the stairs. Now he reached for her hand, and it slid out of his. He tried again, and again it slipped, like trying to hold a fish. Paati was standing at the top of the stairs, frightened, and he could not hold on to her.
"Gecko!" Arjun shouted. "Gecko, I take it back! I take it all back!"

The gecko was on the ceiling, upside down, perfectly still. Its feet were the only things in the whole house not slipping. "Do you, now?" it said. "But friction was slowing you down. It made your legs burn. It wore out your shoes."
"I know," said Arjun, and he was nearly crying. "But it was also what let me hold on."
The gecko blinked once, slowly. And the floor stopped being ice.
Arjun ran to the stairs and took Paati's hand, and her dry, wrinkled fingers held his, and his held hers, and they did not slip. They went down the stairs together, one step at a time.

That morning he pushed his heavy cycle up the hill, and his legs burned, and he did not complain once. At the top, he stopped and put his hand on the warm road and said, very quietly, so nobody would hear: "Thank you."
story.epiphany: Friction is a force between surfaces that slows things down, and it is also what lets us walk, grip, write, tie knots, brake, carry loads and hold hands. The turn is the moment Paati's hand slips. The idea under it: the same force that makes life hard is what lets us hold on to each other.
ask: List everything that went wrong without friction. Can you add more?
Why did the women's water pots slide off?
Arjun said friction 'was also what let me hold on'. What did he mean?
Name one place in your home where you want more friction, and one where you want less.

ideas.idea: The force that slows us is also the force that lets us hold on.
ideas.more: Without friction you couldn't walk, write, tie a knot or hold a cup. Friction also wears things out and turns movement into heat.

ideas.idea: A feeling can become a number.
ideas.more: People always knew a push could be big or small. Measuring it in newtons let scientists compare, predict and build. Turning what we feel into what we can measure is one of science's great tricks.

ideas.idea: You are the same stuff everywhere, but your weight depends on where you stand.
ideas.more: Your mass is how much of you there is. Your weight is how hard a planet pulls you. On the Moon you'd weigh a sixth as much without losing a single gram.

ideas.idea: Balanced forces are everywhere, even when nothing moves.
ideas.more: A book on a table is being pulled down by the whole Earth and pushed up by the table, exactly equally, all the time.

unknowns: Why is ice so slippery? It sounds simple, but scientists are still arguing: is it a thin layer of water on top, is it melting from the pressure or the heat of rubbing, or something about the ice's surface itself? Nobody is sure.
Scientists still cannot fully predict how much friction two surfaces will have just from what they're made of. Friction is one of the oldest puzzles in physics, and it isn't solved.

Who invented the wheel? The oldest wheels found are about 5,000 years old, from Europe and western Asia, but rollers and potter's wheels may be older, and nobody knows who first had the idea, or whether different people had it separately.
